item.title: Could 2026 be the year we start using quantum computers for chemistry?
item.description: Understanding the chemical properties of a molecule is an inherently quantum problem, making quantum computers a good tool for the job – and we may start seeing this take off in 2026

item.title: Here we go again: Retiring coal plant forced to stay open by Trump Admin
item.description: This time, a Colorado plant scheduled to shut down will be kept on standby.

item.title: Einstein Probe detects an X-ray flare from nearby star
item.description: Using the Einstein Probe (EP), astronomers have detected a new X-ray transient event, which turned out to be an X-ray flare from the star PM J23221-0301 located about 150 light years away. The finding was reported in a research paper published December 18 on the arXiv preprint server.

item.title: Wind-battered Lick Observatory rushes to shield historic telescope after dome damage
item.description: Winds exceeding 110 mph that tore across the top of Mount Hamilton early Christmas morning blasted a massive steel protective door off the iconic white dome at Lick Observatory.

item.title: Three supermassive black holes have been spotted merging into one
item.description: Astronomers have found a system of three supermassive black holes, all actively feeding, that appear to be combining into a single system – a rare event that will help elucidate the physics of complex mergers

item.title: Can beavers help heal burn scars after wildfires? Researchers build their own dams to find out
item.description: High in the mountains west of Fort Collins, teams of scientists and engineers are pretending to be beavers.

item.title: Regional temperature records broken across the world in 2025
item.description: Central Asia, the Sahel region and northern Europe experienced their hottest year on record in 2025, according to AFP analysis based on data from the European Copernicus program.

item.title: The duo kite-skiing 4000 kilometres across Antarctica for science
item.description: An explorer and a glaciologist are kite-skiing across Antarctica with a ground-penetrating radar to gather data that will help understand the past and future of the ice sheet
